name: Email me this: a long answer sent to the asker's own inbox
description: A parent texts 'email me this' and the long answer, table or plan lands in that parent's own inbox as plain text; either parent can ask. It is sent from the Gmail address Happy already has unless Tony names another. The only address the send tool accepts is the asker's own: a check in code blocks every other send, and blocks when the check itself fails.
example: Jordan texts: 'Email me that comparison.' The full text arrives in her own inbox as plain text from Happy's address. A send that names anyone else on the To, cc or bcc line, or that goes out as a reply-all, is blocked.
how: One shared mail-out server on the host: gog run as an MCP server for the sending address with its write and Gmail-send flags and only `gmail_send_message` registered, signed in with a send-only grant if the installed gog offers one. It is allowed by name on each parent's own agent, denied on the mail readers and every shared agent, and sits behind the same gate as the mail readers' connector (wave A's blocking rule and the local proxy's Google hosts). The card adds one rule to the house-rules plugin, the send-to-owner rule: a send is blocked unless the caller is a parent's own agent and the one recipient is that agent's owner, read from the family file, with no cc, bcc, reply or reply-all target, send-as alias or HTML body. The check fails closed. Before go-live: T5's send-tool turn, then the roadmap's five seeded ways to change the recipient (the other parent and a reply-all among them) and an injected web page. No send cap.
caveats: The promise that nobody else can be a recipient rests on one in-house rule, and it is not yet shown that the check sees every field that can set a recipient: to, cc and bcc, and also the reply fields, because the upstream page for the mail tool says a send needs 'recipients or a reply-all target'. The seeded sends, a reply-all among them, must all be blocked before this goes live.
The check blocks a wrong recipient; it does not correct it, because the docs describe rewriting parameters for host-owned tools only.
Plain text only: a table arrives as lined-up text, not as a formatted table. A long iMessage already delivers the same text; what this adds is the answer filed in the inbox.

Pinning the recipient does not close every way out: the mailed text is often built from research results, and a link in it can carry private text in its address to whoever runs that site once it is clicked. A link is only as trustworthy as the result it came from.
No send cap: a runaway loop could fill the asker's own inbox until someone notices or the agent's spend cap stops it.
Signing Happy's existing Google account in on the Mac mini for sending is a new use of that account. A send-only grant keeps the token from reading that mailbox, if the installed gog supports it.
unverified: That the blocking check is called for the mail-out server's send tool and is given every field that can set a recipient: the upstream page names recipients, reply context, a reply-all target and send-as aliases as inputs but does not list the tool's input schema, so whether cc and bcc are separate fields is not known (T5's send-tool turn, then the five-way test).
That the check is told which agent is calling, so it can look up that agent's owner; the rule refuses the send when the agent id or the owner lookup is missing (T5).
That the installed gog offers a send-only grant (`gog auth add --gmail-scope send` was read in the upstream command reference) and that the MCP send tool works under it.
That gog's MCP write, Gmail-send and tool-filter flags behave as documented on the installed version; the roadmap lists this as not yet confirmed.
safety: Each parent's own agent holds private data and reads outside content, so its mail way out is pinned in code: the house-rules plugin blocks any send not addressed to the calling agent's owner alone, and blocks when the check fails. No mail reader or shared agent gets the tool. Plain text only, so no remote image can report back.

name: Kids agent (waits for a local model): text with homework hints, chat hours, parent alerts and a nightly digest, then the kitchen speaker
description: Later, each child texts Happy from their own Apple account and gets a helper with no tools and no memory, on a local model, that gives grade-level hints and short explanations and is told not to hand over a finished worksheet; the parents get chat hours per child, a text when a message is flagged for safety or distress (meant to arrive at once; how the plugin sends it is not settled), and an evening digest of what each child asked, delivered only by a route that keeps the child's words off the cloud model (still to be checked). Whether a child may chat with Happy alone, or only with a parent alongside, is a decision to take before building. As a second step the same kids agent answers by voice through the roadmap's kitchen speaker (Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition), with wake word, speech-to-text and text-to-speech running locally so that only text reaches Happy.
example: Trigger: at 21:40 the 8-year-old texts the kids agent and gets a fixed 'time for bed, ask me tomorrow' line. At the kitchen speaker: 'Okay Nabu, why is the sky blue?'
how: Base (F072): `bindings[]` by DM handle to one agent per kid, the minimal profile with `session_status` and `gateway` denied, memory search off, a daily reset and an in-house kid-safety plugin with a local classifier on `before_dispatch` and `message_sending`. Hints (F073): hint-first rules and a grade band in AGENTS.md; no URLs. Hours and alerts (MKT-13): the same plugin gives a fixed reply outside each kid's hours and texts both parents the category and time on a safety label. Digest (G019): a host-side command job summarises the day's sessions on a local model. Speaker (VOX-11): the device, Home Assistant OS in a VM on the Mac, Whisper and Piper through the Wyoming integration, and a kids-only shim in front of the gateway, whose OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint is full operator access.
caveats: Blocked until a local model and local classifiers exist and the kid-safety evals pass, because kids' content never goes to a cloud model or cloud speech.

A local classifier's accuracy on how 8 and 10-year-olds actually write is unproven: false alarms will annoy, misses matter more, and a home system has no human reviewer between the flag and the parent notice.

Common Sense Media rated Google's supervised assistant for under-13s high risk and recommends that children aged 6 to 12 use chatbots only under adult supervision; an alert and an evening digest are a look afterwards, not supervision, so whether a child may chat alone is a decision to take before building.
'Refuse whole-worksheet answers' is a prompt rule, and no source shows a model holds to it when a child pushes.
The alert is a heads-up to parents and not a crisis service, and the parents should be told so.

The speaker has no interim adult version: nothing identifies who is speaking, so without a local model a child's question would reach OpenAI as text, and speech stays in the house only while Home Assistant's own cloud speech option is left off.

The hop from Home Assistant to Happy is unsolved: Home Assistant's official OpenAI integration only talks to OpenAI's own endpoint, and with token auth OpenClaw's chat endpoint gives the caller the full operator scope set and lets the request choose the agent, so the bridge would be a community integration or a self-written kids-only shim.

The speaker adds an always-on VM to patch and back up, Home Assistant itself calls the device a preview, and open-ended questions need Whisper, which Home Assistant recommends only on powerful hardware.
How the safety plugin texts the parents from inside a hook is not settled: no plugin-side send path was found in the hook docs read, so an 'immediate' alert is the aim, not a tested behaviour.

OpenClaw's local-model guide says local models do not come with the hosted providers' safety filters. Keeping the children's chat off the cloud therefore also gives up the vendor's own content filtering, and the local classifier becomes the only filter between the model and a child, which is one more reason the kid-safety evals have to pass first.
corrections: 'OpenAI terms are 13+, no cloud shortcut' could not be confirmed as worded: OpenAI's consumer Terms of Use returned HTTP 403 in this run, and the API page that did open sets no flat 13+ bar. It says personal data of children under 13 must not be processed without zero data retention and that COPPA applies. Keeping kids off the cloud stays the family's rule; store:false was not shown to count as zero data retention.
unverified: Llama Guard 3 as the classifier is the roadmap's choice and appears nowhere in the installed OpenClaw docs (its Ollama library page is among this card's sources).
Whether kids admitted by pairing are refused as approvers; the roadmap itself marks this as untested.
How accurate any local classifier is on questions from 8 and 10 year olds; no evaluation exists yet.
'Refuse whole-worksheet answers' is a prompt rule; no source shows a model holds to it when a child pushes.
A parent asking the same questions from their own chat works today, but that is the parent using the cloud model, not the child.
Whether the Apple on-device model can be called from a host job for an ad hoc summary; the doc gives it an 8,192-token window and 1,024 output tokens and describes utility use only.
Reading the per-agent database from a command job (read-only open or the history RPC) was not tried.

Which session transcript a delivered digest line is copied into: the installed source appends direct scheduled deliveries to a session transcript (dist/delivery-dispatch-awareness-CcGkYFaV.mjs:518), and if that session belongs to a parent's cloud-backed agent, the quoted kid text would reach a cloud model.
Whether ChatGPT's controls changed after the September 2025 launch report; OpenAI's own page returned 403 in this run.
How the plugin sends a proactive message to the parents from inside a hook; G009 covers the agent `message` tool and host jobs, and no plugin-side send path was found in the hook docs read.
Which Home Assistant conversation integration can target a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint in 2026 (the roadmap cites a community one; I did not verify it).
Whisper latency inside a VM on this Mac.
Whether OpenClaw can issue an HTTP credential scoped to one agent.

Whether a trusted-proxy identity in front of the HTTP endpoint could narrow a caller to one agent. With the token auth this gateway uses, the docs say scope headers are ignored and the request's model field selects any agent.
safety: The design keeps the children's content off the cloud: the agent, its classifiers and the digest summariser are local, and with the classifier down the agent answers 'ask a grown-up'. Alerts carry a category, not the child's words. Two points are open. The nightly digest tells the parents what a child asked and is delivered into a parent's chat with Happy; OpenClaw copies a scheduled delivery into a session transcript, and if that session belongs to a parent's cloud-backed agent the child's words would reach the cloud model, so the delivery route has to be checked before the digest quotes anything. And the speaker's bridge: the chat endpoint is equivalent to an operator secret, so the speaker must reach only the tool-less kids agent.

name: Scheduled jobs: three safety switches and one short jobs script
description: Before Happy sends its first scheduled text, three scheduler settings go in: a failed job alerts Tony and not the family, runs missed during a power cut are skipped, and script triggers are off. Every scheduled text is then one job created by one short checked-in script, with its owner's handle read from the family file, a time limit, a tool list, its own daytime hour and its rules in its own message. A job with nothing to say sends nothing.
example: Jordan's 07:00 mail text fails twice in a row: Tony gets one text from Happy saying so and one more when it recovers, and she is not sent the error. After a power cut the 07:00 text does not turn up at 11:40. To quieten a text, Tony switches that one job off.
how: Config first: `cron.failureAlert` with Tony's handle as its destination, `cron.skipMissedJobs: true`, `cron.triggers.enabled: false`. Then test T3: happy-inspect gains one read-only line, `automations list --all --json`, and one throwaway job is added twice under the same `--declaration-key` with a changed message; one job afterwards means one add line per job, two means a name-keyed comparison is kept. Then one short checked-in jobs script, applied through the deploy path as the happy user. Every real job the script declares (not T3's throwaway probes) carries `--agent`, `--tz` and `--timeout-seconds`; a job whose text is delivered also carries `--to` (the owner's handle read from family.json5, never typed in) and `--announce`, and a test job that must send nothing is declared with `--no-deliver`. A job that calls the model also carries an explicit `--tools` list and no `--light-context`, so the hard rules load on every run; its message holds its rules: begin with the job's label, answer `NO_REPLY` when there is nothing to say. A text that needs no model is a `--command-argv` job. Something for both parents is two jobs, one each. No house-rules rule.
caveats: Failed-job alerts reach Tony as an iMessage from Happy, a deliberate exception to his 'alerts by ntfy' decision: OpenClaw's chat notice carries only a tidied cause, while its webhook would post the raw error text to an outside push service. If iMessage itself is down, the existing Grafana alerts still reach him by ntfy.

Alerts start after 2 failures in a row with a 1-hour cooldown. A recurring job is switched off after 10 failures in a row and then disappears from the default job list, which is why the inspect line lists every job, disabled ones included. Without a time limit of its own a model job is bounded only by a 60-minute watchdog, so the script sets one on every job.

Switching script triggers off does not stop the no-model jobs that other cards add through this script: OpenClaw's docs list a command job as a separate kind from the script payloads, condition triggers and stream schedules that the switch turns off.

After a reboot with FileVault locked nothing fires and nothing alerts; the healthchecks dead-man switch stays the only signal for a Mac that is off. One-off reminders still catch up after an outage even with missed runs skipped.

Given up with this form: per-person on and off switches in the family file, automatic clean-up of jobs that no longer match it, and any enforced daily cap or quiet hours. A changed job is applied again by the script if test T3 shows that a job declared again under the same key is updated in place (the wave A runbook read that in the installed code); otherwise it is edited by hand; to quieten Happy, Tony switches a job off or a parent silences the thread on the phone. The comparing generator comes back when the script holds more jobs than can be read at a glance.

Reminders Tony sets in chat (F007) are jobs outside the script; the inspect listing shows them beside the scripted ones. The script creates Jordan's jobs too, so her scheduled texts need no command right of her own.
corrections: Diffing against 'automations list --json' is not enough: the list shows enabled jobs only unless --all is passed, so a job disabled by a mute would look missing and be created twice. Use 'automations list --all --json'.
unverified: T3: whether a command run as the happy user through the deploy path reaches the scheduler's job list at all; job changes need the admin operator scope, and nothing in Tony's account calls the Gateway today except the two installed scripts.
T3: whether adding a job twice under the same `--declaration-key` updates it or doubles it; the flag was read in the installed code, is not described on the CLI doc page, and nothing was run.
That the first text Happy sends by itself is delivered on this version: M1's sign-off records that replies needed a workaround, so T3's throwaway job also announces one fixed line to Tony.
That a job answering `NO_REPLY` sends nothing and raises no failure alert on iMessage: documented, not tried.

That a failed job of Jordan's alerts Tony and nobody else once the global destination is set (the documented route order, not tried), and where the auto-disable notice lands: the docs say the owning agent receives it even when failure alerts are off, so it may reach the family member's thread and not Tony's.
safety: Only restrictive. Script triggers are off before any agent holds the scheduling tool, because they would run with the owning agent's full tool policy. Every job's text goes to its owner alone, whose handle the script reads from the family file; each job has a time limit, and a model job a tool list. Failure alerts go to Tony, not into another person's thread.

name: Stopping and checking Happy by text: the built-in commands on one printed sheet
description: One printed sheet of what already stops and checks Happy, with nothing new built: for Tony, a text that says only 'stop' ends the answer in progress, /new starts a clean chat, and /status, /usage and /tools show health, cost and what Happy can do (documented; not yet tried on iMessage, so the sheet is worded from a five-text test). Jordan is not a command owner, so for her only /new and /reset work; her stop is to tell Tony or, at home, to shut the Mac mini down. The sheet also says what Happy's error line means when the model is down, and what to do about a lost phone.
example: Tony texts 'stop' when a long answer is heading the wrong way, then '/new'. When a scheduled text starts arriving twice, Jordan tells Tony, and he switches the scheduler off at the Mac.
how: No plugin, no in-house phrase and no rule in the house-rules plugin. First test T8: from his own phone Tony sends 'stop' during a long answer, then /new, /status, /usage and /tools, and notes what comes back; one failed turn is provoked on an eval-only copy of an agent to read the error line a parent would see. The sheet is written from what he saw: the commands that work for Tony (no `commands.allowFrom` entry is added for Jordan), /new and /reset for Jordan, which words stop one answer, and what stops everything: Tony at the Mac, `cron.enabled: false`, then `openclaw gateway stop`. Lost phone, three lines: Find My Lost Mode; Tony removes the handle in family.json5 and redeploys; `openclaw devices revoke` if that phone ever ran the app. The sheet also says what each scheduled text is and how Tony switches it off, what Happy's error line means, and the photos card's house-rule line (F002).
caveats: With an owner list set and no `commands.allowFrom`, OpenClaw gives the second parent /new and /reset only: her /stop, a bare 'stop', /status, /usage and /tools are dropped without a reply (read from the installed docs and code, not tried from her phone).
/stop and the built-in stop words end one answer in one chat and pause no scheduled job, so the sheet says which words stop one answer and which steps stop everything.

OpenClaw's stop list has 43 fixed phrases and includes everyday words such as 'exit', 'halt' and 'do not do that': a text that is only one of them ends the answer in progress instead of reaching Happy.

Given up with this form: one text from either parent that halts everything while Tony cannot be reached, and a lock-out by text for a lost phone. The phone's own lock screen and Lost Mode cover that gap unless the phone was lost unlocked, and only removing the handle and redeploying ends that handle's approver rights.
Shutting the Mac mini down is a stop Jordan cannot undo: after a restart it waits at the disk-unlock screen and Happy stays down until Tony unlocks it.
/usage shows local estimates and not the provider's bill, /status and /tools may run long in an iMessage bubble, and /btw and /loop stay off the sheet.
corrections: 'Freeze every outbound write' is fail-closed only for tool calls. The phrase matcher and the message_sending check both log and continue when their handler throws or times out, so a broken plugin lets the phrase reach the model and lets scheduled announce texts out. The levels that do not depend on plugin code are the scheduler switch and stopping the Gateway.
unverified: T8: what the built-in stop words and /new, /status, /usage and /tools actually return on iMessage, and how /status and /tools render in a bubble; read from the docs and the code, never tried.
T8: the exact line a parent sees on iMessage when a turn fails because the model is down; the docs describe it, it has not been seen.
That a non-owner admitted sender is limited to /new and /reset: read from the installed docs and source, not tried from the second parent's phone.
Whether switching the scheduler off stops a job already running, and whether switching it back needs a restart (the hot-reload table says no; the automation troubleshooting page says restart).
safety: Nothing is built or granted: no plugin, no new command right, no change to who is admitted. Jordan is not authorised for commands, so the commands and directives that authorisation would open (/tts, /compact, /model among them) stay closed to her. Stopping everything and removing a handle stay actions Tony takes at the Mac; /restart and /update stay off.

name: Weather by the hour: the hourly forecast for home
description: Ask whether it will rain at home on Saturday morning and get the chance of rain hour by hour, with any active weather alert for home, straight from the National Weather Service. The evening text and the day-out planner use the same hourly line.
example: Jordan texts: 'Will it rain at home on Saturday between 9 and noon?' Happy answers with the hourly chance of rain for those hours and any active alert for home.
how: Extend the in-house home_weather plugin: follow `forecastHourly` from the points lookup the tool already makes, so the tool can also answer hour by hour, on the same pinned host (api.weather.gov), with the same refusal of redirects and of any forecast address on another host. Active alerts are already fetched with every forecast and stay as they are. Not built: a snowfall figure from the raw gridpoint endpoint, and an alert id in the output. The plugin's own tests are extended with a recorded hourly response, and one live question about rain on a given afternoon is answered by the hour before it goes live. No house-rules rule.
caveats: Apple's Weather app can already send a notification when rain or snow is about to start or stop, and for government-issued severe-weather alerts at a saved location; Apple notes this is not offered in every country or region. This tool earns its place as the hourly rain line for the evening text (F014) and the day-out planner (F028), and for questions asked inside a Happy conversation.
The National Weather Service hourly forecast reaches seven days ahead, so a question about a day further out gets no hour-by-hour answer until the date comes into range.
The tool knows only the home point, so it cannot answer for a field or a venue somewhere else; for other places Happy falls back to web search.

No snowfall amount in numbers on day one. The field exists in the raw gridpoint data, in millimetres over mostly six-hour intervals, so it would not give an hour-by-hour amount; the forecaster's own text for each period still comes through. It is added only if a first snow forecast shows the need.
unverified: What a live hourly response for the home point looks like: the sources cite the weather service's documentation, not a response read for home. The go-live check (one live question about rain on a given afternoon, answered by the hour) settles it.
NWS publishes no numeric rate limit, so the 10-minute cache is a design choice rather than an NWS rule.
Whether Apple's Weather notifications are offered and switched on for the home location on each parent's iPhone: the Apple page read was the Mac Weather guide, and the iPhone guide did not render.
safety: Read-only public data from one pinned government host. A lookup sends the home's coordinates and the header that identifies the app, as the National Weather Service asks, and nothing else about the family. What comes back is outside content from a single government source; the tool only reads, and cannot write anything or message anyone.

name: School lines first in the weekday 07:00 mail text
description: Each parent whose Gmail is connected gets a weekday 07:00 mail text (G015) that opens with the school lines: a short list of the last day's school and activity mail about the two children, with dates spelled out and things to do first. The model picks out the school mail from the whole inbox, with the school's sender addresses as a hint and not as a filter, and passes on no links. Length and layout are tuned on the first two weeks of real mail.
example: Trigger: the weekday 07:00 mail text, one to each parent from that parent's own inbox. After the job's own label it opens with the school lines, for example: 'Mail. School: picture day is Thursday 15 October, order form due Wednesday 14 October; the third-grader's trip slip is due Friday 16 October.' The other mail lines follow in the same text.
how: No separate job, no sender list, no check on the search and no stored last-run marker. The school lines are one instruction in the message of the weekday 07:00 job on each parent's mail reader (G015). The short jobs script (G003) creates that job with the owner's handle read from the family file, a time limit and a tool list of Gmail read tools only. The instruction: from the last day's mail (three days on a Monday), list first what comes from the school district, teachers, teams and activities, each date spelled out, the sender named, no links. One hint line carries the school's sender addresses, which Tony provides at execution. Mail from other senders that is plainly school mail is still listed. After go-live, read the first two weeks of digests to see which school systems actually write; only then change a platform's own digest setting, and only for one that shows up.
caveats: The model, not a list, decides what counts as school mail, so a school mail can be missed or a non-school mail included. No links are passed on; the parent opens the mail in Gmail.
A school mail that arrives during the day is reported the next morning; there is no afternoon text. Whether the school already texts or pushes urgent notices to the parents' phones is not on record.

Both parents receive the same school mail, so the school lines in the two texts will mostly match. Each is built from its owner's inbox, and nothing is sent from one parent's reader to the other parent.

If a school system emails grades or attendance, that is a child's education record, and it reaches the cloud model with the rest of the mail. Attachments are not opened, so a newsletter sent as a PDF or a picture shows up as a subject line only.

A day-before reminder is not wired from the text: the mail reader holds no reminder tool on purpose, because it reads outside mail. Tony types the reminder to his own agent once timed reminders exist (F007); that works for Tony only, because Jordan is not a command owner.
Which school systems send this family mail is not on record, so nothing is changed on any school platform until real digests show which ones write.
corrections: 'IMAP passes body text only' is slightly off: the plugin's prompt also lists attachment file names (dist/extensions/imap/index.js:55735). Contents of attached PDFs or images are still not passed, so flyer attachments remain unread.
'school-mail-ro MCP is gog (Gmail)' needs no wrapper code on the Gmail path: upstream gogcli ships a read-only stdio MCP server (`gog mcp`).
The built-in scheduling tool is listed as `automations`, with `cron` kept as an alias (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:73).
unverified: Which school systems send this family mail, and whether the school uses Google Classroom: seen in the first two weeks of real digests.
Whether the school already texts or pushes urgent notices to the parents' phones.
How well the model picks out school mail from a day's inbox: not measured; the first hand-started digests are read against the inbox for misses.
gog is not installed, so its Gmail read tools, and what they return for attachments, come from upstream docs.

Whether a parent's own agent can see or quote the morning text when the parent replies to it: checked at go-live with G015. If it can, Tony signs that as the same departure from the roadmap as the lookup.
safety: School mail is outside content. Only its owner's mail reader reads it: Gmail read tools only, no web, file, send or message tool. Once the lookup (G015) is on, the owner's own agent is allowed the same three tools so that the reader it starts can use them, and is told never to use them itself. Its scheduled text goes to its owner alone, and the lookup (G015) returns an answer to that owner's own agent only when the parent asks. No links are relayed. The card needs no rule in the house-rules plugin. Mail text goes to the cloud model, as Tony allowed on 12 Oct.

name: Childcare coverage planner: no-school days and summer weeks
description: A grid of the weekdays the two children have no school (teacher days, breaks, early releases, summer weeks) against who covers each one. Either parent adds or changes cover by text and can ask what is still open, and a monthly text lists the open days and weeks to each parent who has it switched on, staying silent when nothing is open. The parents register and pay for anything themselves.
example: Trigger: the monthly text. Each parent who has it switched on gets, for example: 'Coverage still open: Friday 6 November, both children; the week of 5 July for the kindergartner.' Jordan then texts her own Happy: 'the week of 5 July is covered, mark it booked', and the next answer either parent gets shows it.
how: This card adds one coverage table and three tools (add, change, list) to the household database plugin (F031) and keeps no store of its own. A row holds a date range, which child, a status (open, pencilled, booked, paid) and a short who-covers label; the tools accept only those typed fields. No-school days come from the school district's calendar: through the calendar tool (F009) once the family Google calendar is subscribed to its feed, or from a photo or PDF (F002). The parent's agent lists the days and writes rows only after a yes. One monthly job per parent who has it switched on, from the jobs script (G003) and holding only the list tool, texts the open rows to its owner under its own label, or answers `NO_REPLY`. Registration dates are ordinary reminders (F007, Tony only); camp options are an ordinary question to the research helper (F019). Not built: weekly pre-break jobs, page watches, the receipts list, a house-rules rule.
depends_on: F031 household database in its smallest form: this card adds its one coverage table and its three tools there; the rows are shared data both parents' agents write, so they live there and nowhere else

F009 read-only calendar, with the family Google calendar subscribed to the school district's calendar feed; or F002 photo and PDF reading, for a district calendar that exists only as a PDF. Tony provides the feed link or the PDF at execution
G003 in its simplified form: the jobs script creates the monthly text, one job per parent who has it switched on
Tony provides at execution: the day and hour of the monthly text, and which of the two parents have it switched on (one job each)
Tony provides a short label for each of the two children at execution (not a full name; the same labels the dose log, CRT-10, uses)
Optional, not needed for the grid: F007 reminders for registration dates (Tony only, since Jordan is not a command owner) and F019 research helper for camp options
caveats: The planner earns its keep only if both parents have to arrange cover on those days. A shared spreadsheet does the grid; the gain here is asking in the thread and the monthly list of what is open.
Registration is a booking and a payment: Happy stops at the reminder and the link, and the parents register and pay.
Reminders for registration dates work for Tony only, because Jordan is not a command owner; when she asks, Happy lists the dates and she sets them on her phone.

Camp sites are often script-heavy or bot-walled, so an answer about camp options may say 'could not verify'; the parent pastes the dates. Such a question carries ages, weeks and a distance to the research helper, never names or the school.
The rows are shared between the two adults by design. Values stay short and typed (a date range, a status, a label), not text lifted from a page or a flyer.
No weekly texts before a break and no watch on a camp's registration page; either is added only after the monthly text has proved useful and a parent asks.
safety: Rows are written only through the database plugin's tools, which accept in code only typed fields: dates, a child's label, one of four statuses and a short label. The district calendar or flyer is outside content, so rows are written only after a yes. The monthly job holds one read tool and texts only its owner. Nothing is registered, booked or paid.
unverified: Whether the school district publishes a calendar feed or only a PDF.
That events from a calendar subscribed by link are returned through the Google Calendar API, and so through gog's calendar tool.
That a tool from the in-house household-database plugin can be named in a job's tool list; the installed docs show the `<server>__<tool>` form for MCP servers only.
That the monthly job on an empty grid sends nothing and raises no failure alert: a hand-started run before go-live shows it.
